It can be difficult to change the narrative in sport. Take Cardiff City and their rivalry with Swansea City.

For years, a certain idea had taken hold, that the Swans - their players, staff, the club as a whole - had a better understanding of what the south Wales derby meant, and that innate grasp of its significance had given them the upper hand.

Results have supported the theory. Since a nine-year period at the start of this century where there were no derbies, Swansea have won 11 out of 21 and become the first team in the fixture's century-long history to do the double – that is, to win both league meetings in one season – before repeating the feat the following campaign.
Once a pattern is set in motion, it can take some stopping but, by winning their past two home derbies, Cardiff felt the tide might have been turning.
Granted, the most recent of those triumphs still ended with their relegation to League One two seasons ago, but there was at least a feeling that the hoodoo had been lifted.

Nearly two years have passed since the last south Wales derby. In that time, Cardiff have made an instant return to the Championship under head coach Brian Barry-Murphy, who has introduced a refreshingly bold and attacking style of play, built around a core of young local players.
They are still behind their neighbours, though.
Cardiff travel to Swansea on Sunday 17th in the table, nine places and nine points adrift of their opponents.

The Bluebirds have caught the eye with their performances this season but, for all their ambition and stylish dominance of possession, the defensive risks that come attached mean that they are still searching for a first away win of the campaign.

You have to go back nine derbies for the last time Cardiff won in Swansea, and a decade further back again for the last time they triumphed there with fans present.
What an opportunity this weekend's reunion presents, then, to shift another narrative.
"You have to accept it's a different game," says Barry-Murphy, preparing for his first south Wales derby.
"It's not a normal game, and I think if you try to make out as if it's just another game, you're preparing for something that's not going to happen.
"This is a totally different fixture for our players because the atmosphere is going to be totally different.
"We have to show that we have the characteristics and personality to perform the way we want to perform in that heat of battle and show who we want to be as a team.
"We're a very aggressive team and have a lot of daring players who play on the front foot. Our intention on Sunday, despite whatever the opposition do, is to show that version of ourselves."
